吉田稔麿.note: Chōshū loyalist (1841–1864), a favored pupil of Yoshida Shōin; killed at twenty-four in the Ikedaya fight.

宮部鼎蔵.note: Higo loyalist (1820–1864), a leading strategist of the cause; died at the Ikedaya.

松田重助.note: Higo loyalist, killed at the Ikedaya.

北添佶麿.note: Tosa loyalist, cut down at the head of the Ikedaya stairs. The given name 佶麿 is read Yoshimaro.

望月亀弥太.note: Tosa loyalist, an associate of Sakamoto Ryōma; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly in the street.

野老山.note: Tokoroyama Gokichirō, Tosa loyalist; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly before the locked Chōshū gate.

大高又次郎.note: Banshū loyalist and leather-armorer; killed at the Ikedaya.

玉虫左大夫.note: A Sendai clansman and diarist (1823–1869); his intelligence-record Kanbu Tsūki preserves these figures. Also written 玉虫左太夫.

惣兵衛.note: Ikedaya Sōbei, keeper of the inn; he died in prison after the affair.

奥沢新三郎.note: The one Shinsengumi corpsman killed outright at the Ikedaya.

安藤早太郎.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

新田革左衛門.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

山田信道.note: Matsuda Jūsuke’s younger brother, later governor of Kyōto Prefecture, who raised the memorial to the Ikedaya dead.

ch23.anchor: A frontage of three and a half ken
ch23.note: The ken was a length of about 1.8 meters and the shaku about 30 centimeters, so the inn ran some 6.3 meters across the front and 27 deep, and the stair-corridor upstairs (below) a bare 90 centimeters wide — the narrowness that let a handful of men hold it. Shiba’s parenthesis is a modern traveler’s: the Ikedaya was pulled down in 1931 and a concrete inn stood on the site when he wrote.

ch23.anchor: the soba shop in the case of the Akō rōnin
ch23.note: The forty-seven rōnin of Akō, heroes of the most famous vendetta in Japanese history, are remembered as mustering at a soba (buckwheat-noodle) shop near their target on the night of their raid in 1703. Shiba likens the Gion meeting-house, where the corps put on its armor, to that staging-point.

Katsura Kogorō is the later Kido Takayoshi (see the glossary), one of the architects of the Restoration; the passages quoted are from his own diary. His being away from the Ikedaya when the corps struck is historical, and of a piece with a career of hairbreadth escapes that earned him the by-name “Kogorō the bolter.”

ch23.anchor: half of these would likely have held high office in the Restoration government
ch23.note: The roster is historical, and Shiba’s claim is sober rather than rhetorical. Yoshida Toshimaro, dead at twenty-four, was among the ablest pupils of Yoshida Shōin, the Chōshū teacher whose students went on to lead the Restoration; Miyabe Teizō was the senior Higo strategist of the cause. The raid is often said to have set the loyalist movement back by years by cutting down such men. Corroborated.

Kondō’s prized blade, a Nagasone Kotetsu (see the glossary). He wrote home that it came through the night’s fighting unbent while his men’s swords broke; whether his Kotetsu was a true work of that much-forged smith or one of the many fakes has been argued ever since.

Tamamushi Sadayū (1823–1869), a Sendai clansman who had crossed the Pacific with the 1860 embassy to the United States, kept in his Kanbu Tsūki a running record of the doings of court, shogunate, and clans; it is a standard source for these years. The figures that follow are his.

ch23.anchor: The dead on the spot on the men-of-purpose side were seven
ch23.note: The tallies differ across the sources: the loyalist dead are variously given as seven, eight, or nine on the night, with more dying later of wounds, and the captured at some twenty to twenty-three. Shiba follows one set of figures; the exact count was disputed from the first, both sides having reason to shade it.
